faq.answer: Heavy group contribution does not prove social Nine. Paid duties, mutual aid, family obligation, or exclusion risk may require service; compare whether personal priorities disappear even when membership and voice are secure.
faq.question: Does heavy group contribution prove social Nine?

faq.answer: Belonging can be tested without blaming accommodation by recording power, duty, and consequences of refusal. Silence under credible exclusion is a safety response, while safe dissent provides a cleaner comparison.
faq.question: How can belonging be tested without blaming accommodation?

faq.answer: A counterexample weakens the participation hypothesis when the person declines optional labor, protects a personal commitment, states disagreement, and stays connected without later compensating through invisible work.
faq.question: Which counterexample weakens the participation hypothesis?

sections.body_md: Test whether participation protects connection while personal priorities repeatedly become less visible. High contribution alone is not evidence because groups often depend on legitimate shared labor.
sections.title: Observe belonging through contribution

sections.body_md: Observe the same person in one group where dissent is safe and another where membership, income, or support may be lost. If silence follows risk, power explains more than subtype language.
sections.title: Compare secure membership with exclusion risk

sections.body_md: Social instinct here is a traditional attention comparison and does not describe bodily mechanisms or a fixed group-response system. Belonging needs and institutional consequences remain concrete.
sections.title: Keep social attention conceptual

sections.body_md: A socially active organizer may still postpone their own agenda by carrying collective needs. Visibility, competence, and enthusiasm do not rule the hypothesis in or out.
sections.title: Allow public energy and leadership

sections.body_md: Employment duties, family obligation, mutual-aid norms, migration, discrimination, language status, accessibility, and dependency can make participation necessary rather than identity-driven.
sections.title: Check role, culture, and unequal voice

sections.body_md: Confidence should fall when the person declines nonessential group work, keeps a personal commitment, states dissent, and remains connected without compensating through hidden extra labor.
sections.title: Test belonging after a bounded refusal

sections.body_md: Instrument-specific evidence does not prove universal subtype structure or cross-cultural equivalence. Use contribution, voice, and membership records only as tentative comparisons.
sections.title: Limit claims to revisable observations

sections.body_md:
Duration: 6

Context: Across six days, select one group task, one meeting dissent, and one request that conflicts with a protected personal commitment.

Observable signal: Record role duty, volunteered labor, speaking time, stated preference, exclusion risk, response to refusal, and whether personal time remains protected.

Page-specific signal: Compare contribution and dissent in a secure group with behavior where income, care, status, or community access depends on compliance.

Alternative explanation: Check job description, collective norms, minority stress, migration, language access, disability, family duty, and credible exclusion.

Reflection prompt: Name one refusal that preserved belonging and one silence shaped by real power, then adjust the social hypothesis without blaming the person.

seo.description: Type Nine social is a traditional secondary hypothesis linking a core-Nine stability pattern with participation, shared workload, group rhythm, belonging, and the risk of muting a personal agenda. It does not describe bodily mechanisms. Service may instead reflect job duty, collective culture, mutual aid, exclusion risk, minority stress, or unequal access to voice.
seo.title: Type Nine social: belonging through participation as a secondary hypothesis
